Analysis by Richard Cowan 

An Associated Press – or Absurd Propaganda – story about proposed laws to ban the hallucinogen Salvia Divinorum demonstrates how prohibition really works.

See 

Negligent Journalism: Reader Beware or A Right to Expect More? The Drug Czar Says He Is “Subject to the Scrutiny of the Press.” The Significance of the Ultimate Lies. Analysis by Richard Cowan 

First comes the sensationalist headline, variously “The New Pot” or “The Next Marijuana.” What the hell does that mean? 

Like cannabis, Salvia is a plant, parts of which are psychoactive, but marijuana is not really a hallucinogen, but then jackasses and journalists are both mammals and begin with a J. And politicians and polecats… But never mind, one should not think too much… about whatever… at least not if you want to have a career in journalism or politics. 

Second comes the incitement for teenagers to try it: 

“On websites touting the mind-blowing powers of Salvia divinorum, come-ons to buy the hallucinogenic herb are accompanied by warnings: "Time is running out!" and "stock up while you still can." 

What redblooded American could resist that? And if you call in the next 15 minutes, we will double your order… Ohmygawdd! Ohmygawdd! 

The comes the “hard journalism.” 

“That's because salvia is being targeted by lawmakers concerned that the inexpensive and easy-to-obtain plant could become the next marijuana. Eight states have already placed restrictions on salvia, and 16 others, including Florida, are considering a ban or have previously. 

Then comes the unintended irony, quoting a clueless politician, who doesn’t understand what she is saying: 

"As soon as we make one drug illegal, kids start looking around for other drugs they can buy legally. This is just the next one," said Florida state Rep. Mary Brandenburg, who has introduced a bill to make possession of salvia a felony punishable by up to five years in prison”.

 

I have it on good authority that Rep. Brandenburg did not even know how to pronounce it. 

“Some say legislators are overreacting to a minor problem, but no one disputes that the plant impairs judgment and the ability to drive.”

Like over-the-counter cold remedies? 

See 

Two More Stories from The UK That We Couldn’t Make Up: 10,000 Scots Addicted To Dangerous Over-The-Counter Drugs and Bristol Police Drunk and Lewd At “Anti-Drug” Benefit. 

“Native to Mexico and still grown there, Salvia divinorum is generally smoked but can also be chewed or made into a tea and drunk.” 

Well, we have had so much success banning other things from Mexico, maybe that is the reason that it is the “next marijuana.” How many Mexicans will be killed fighting over the Salvia business, once it is illegal to grow it here? 

See 

Walters Agrees to Help Major Mexican Organized Crime By Prosecuting More Small Marijuana Smugglers. Lock My People Up, Says Mexican AG. The Drug War Really Is About Marijuana. 

“Called nicknames like Sally-D, Magic Mint and Diviner's Sage, salvia is a hallucinogen that gives users an out-of-body sense of traveling through time and space or merging with inanimate objects. Unlike hallucinogens like LSD or PCP, however, salvia's effects last for a shorter time, generally up to an hour.” 

Cooool!!! 

“It is not the same as the ornamental garden plant known as Salvia.” That reminds me of the narks cutting down Japanese Maple plants, that look sort of like cannabis, but are purple. 

“No known deaths have been attributed to salvia's use, but it was listed as a factor in one Delaware teen's suicide two years ago.” 

See 

Meanwhile UK Painkillers Kill 2,000 Per Year. But They Are Sold Over-the-Counter So They Must Be Safe! 

“Salvia's short-lasting effects and fact that it is currently legal may make it seem more appealing to teens, lawmakers say.” 

Is that’s why more kids have stopped using cigarettes than stopped using marijuana?

See 

T’was Another Great Victory. Teen Marijuana Use Down; Oxy Use Up. Teen Cigarette Use Went Down More Than Teen Marijuana Use. 

“In the Delaware suicide, the boy's mother told reporters that salvia made his mood darker but he justified its use by citing its legality. According to reports, the autopsy found no traces of the drug in his system, but the medical examiner listed it as a contributing cause.”

See 

Study Finds That Association Between "Cannabis Abuse" and Suicide Related To Other Problems 

“Mike Strain, Louisiana's Agriculture and Forestry Commissioner and former legislator, helped his state in 2005 become the first to make salvia illegal, along with a number of other plants. He said the response has been largely positive. 

"I got some hostile e-mails from people who sold these products," Strain said. "You don't make everybody happy when you outlaw drugs. You save one child and it's worth it." 

You save one child’s life and it is worth it? Define “it”, please. Is “it” arresting millions of people? Is “it” putting salvia and marijuana in the same market with meth? Is “it” having more prisoners than any other country in the world? Is “it” causing chaos in Mexico, Colombia and Afghanistan? 

But we all look to Louisiana for moral and scientific leadership, and especially on drug policies from their agriculture and forestry experts. 

“An ounce of salvia leaves sells for around $30 on the Internet. A liquid extract from the plant, salvinorin A, is also sold in various strengths labeled "5x" through "60x." A gram of the 5x strength, about the weight of a plastic pen cap, is about $12 while 60x strength is around $65. And in some cases the extract comes in flavors including apple, strawberry and spearmint.” 

Mmmm! Apple, strawberry and spearmint! 

“Moreover, it's hard to say how widespread the use of salvia is. National and state surveys on drug use don't include salvia, and because it is legal in most states, law enforcement officials don't compile statistics, either.

 

San Diego State University last year surveyed more than 1,500 students and found that 4% of participants reported using salvia in the past year.

 

Brandenburg's bill would make salvia and its extract controlled substances in the same class as marijuana and LSD. 

Florida state Sen. Evelyn Lynn, whose committee planned to study the Salvia bill Tuesday, said the drug should be criminalized.

 

"I'd rather be at the front edge of preventing the dangers of the drug than waiting until we are the 40th or more," she said. 

See 

Prophylactic State Violence: The Arrogance and Ignorance of Psychiatric Quackery. Bad Science, Worse Ethics -- Analysis by Richard Cowan

Et cetera, et cetera... 

Said the Queen in Alice in Wonderland: Sentence first -- verdict afterwards.
